content: The guidelines for the treatment of skin and oral conditions associated with HIV in children and adults, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2014, include the following key points: 1. Seborrhoeic Dermatitis: Mild Form: Characterized by scalp scaling or mild to marked erythema of the eyebrows, eyelashes, and nasolabial folds. Severe Form: Involves multiple body sites, including the face, chest, mid-back, axillae, and groin, with marked erythema and extensive greasy scaling. It may also involve the entire body (erythrodermic). Note: Cradle cap in newborns is excluded from these guidelines. 5. Tinea Infections: Tinea refers to dermatophyte infections of keratinized tissue, such as skin (e.g., tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea faciei, tinea pedis, tinea manuum), hair (tinea capitis), or nails (tinea unguium). Extensive tinea involves infection of the hair or nails or large areas of the body. 6. Molluscum Contagiosum: Extensive cases involve a large number of lesions (possibly more than 30) affecting more than one body site (e.g., face and trunk, or trunk and genitalia). Unusual distribution includes extragenital sites in adults and genital involvement in children, as well as involvement of mucocutaneous junctions. 7. Herpes Zoster: Caused by the varicella-zoster virus, it presents as painful clusters of vesicles on an erythematous base, distributed over a single dermatome (or multiple dermatomes), typically unilateral and not crossing the midline. Disseminated zoster, which affects three or more dermatomes or presents with scattered vesicles outside the primary dermatome, occurs in immunocompromised individuals and can be difficult to distinguish from varicella. 8. Scabies: Classified as mild (10 lesions or fewer), moderate (11–49 lesions), severe (50 or more lesions), or crusted. Crusted scabies is a highly infectious, extreme form due to profuse mite proliferation, often seen in immunocompromised, elderly, or debilitated individuals. It presents with widespread scaly patches, crusted lesions, and thickened, discolored fingernails. Itching may be minimal or absent. 9. Topical Corticosteroids: Corticosteroids are anti-inflammatory drugs, often synthetic forms of cortisone, a hormone produced by the adrenal glands. They can be administered orally, by injection, or topically as creams or ointments. Common systemic steroids include prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone. 10. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): These are severe, potentially life-threatening disorders often triggered by medications. They may involve one or more mucous membranes (oral, genital, or conjunctival). Erythema Multiforme: Detachment of less than 10% of the body surface area, with localized typical or raised atypical target lesions. SJS: Detachment of less than 10% of the body surface area, with widespread macules or flat atypical targets. Overlap SJS-TEN: Detachment of 10–30% of the body surface area, with widespread macules or flat atypical targets. TEN with Spots: Detachment of more than 30% of the body surface area, with widespread macules or flat atypical targets. TEN without Spots: Detachment of more than 30% of the body surface area, with large epidermal sheets and no macules or targets. 11. Thrush (Candidiasis): Refers to candidiasis of the mouth, throat, or vagina. 12.
